title: SSRIs Lead To More Suicidal Behavior Compared to DBT in Borderline Personality Disorder
subtitle: Alternate title: "do you mean feeling less of everything doesn't keep you alive?"
body_html:
I’ve written about the data on the treatment of borderline personality disorder before. There is a whole range of effective treatments. All of those effective treatments are psychotherapies. None of them is a drug. If you are looking for a concise review of most psychiatric drugs, I’d encourage you to check out my book, Inessential Pharmacology (Amazon affiliate link). It makes a lackluster holiday gift! After all, some of the most notoriously bad research ever conducted has been in the potential pharmacological treatment of Borderline Personality Disorder.

I’ve previously reviewed what works for Borderline Personality Disorder (therapy), and covered the NYTimes obsession with one therapy, DBT:

However, today, I return to you, dear readers, with more news. A host of august and fancy researchers have compared DBT therapy and SSRIs in BPD using the most crucial outcome one could evaluate—suicidal behavior.

One of those researchers (J. John Mann, M.D.) is so fancy that he personally stuck a needle in my spine when I was 20 years old, when I was a research subject of his, back when he was slumming it in a clinical trial with bipolar patients like your author at Columbia.

The new study, published in AJP, is as follows:

Let’s dig in. I have some things to say…

The authors compared the efficacy of 6 months of dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) to 6 months of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors with clinical management (SSRI/M) in reducing suicide-related events (SREs), suicide attempts, nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), and related clinical outcomes in individuals diagnosed with borderline personality disorder.

This was a relatively older sample with an average age of 30 (for BPD) and overwhelmingly female:

Participants 18–55 years of age were recruited through advertisements, mailings, social media, websites, and local psychiatric emergency, inpatient, and outpatient departments. Study enrollment, treatment, and follow-up occurred between 2009 and 2014.

This data is all pre-pandemic—I’m not sure it means much. Table One is pretty slim:

There are no statistical differences between the groups on the few items presented above. That is enough to tell me the randomization was probably successful! The authors push a bunch of data to table two, which should probably be in table one, so that we can check! The thing I’m looking at is the far-right column—p-values for any of these items below 0.051 would suggest that the groups differ at baseline, and thus the attempt at random assignment failed. Crucially, this didn’t happen.

The SSRI/M and DBT groups were just as likely to have attempted suicide, self-injured, or have any range of other problems, and the severity of those problems was also “close enough” with no statistical difference between groups.

Learn to read Table 1 here. This other article does a good job, too.

I belabor this point not just for educational value, but because prior BPD studies have failed in this regard spectacuraly2, which can lead to regression to the mean, and the appearance of a difference in a treatment that is really due to a difference between the groups at baseline. Data points that start far from the average will become more average over time. We’ve known this since the very birth of statistics, thanks to Francis Galton, whom I wrote about previously here.

The inclusion screening process reads as rigorous:

Potential participants were screened initially by telephone, and then in person by two doctoral-level clinicians to verify the following inclusion criteria: BPD diagnosis; suicidal ideation within the past week; at least one episode of NSSI, suicide attempt, or suicide-related behavior in the past 6 months, and another of these behaviors within the past year; determined to be safe as an outpatient; and not receiving effective treatment elsewhere.

Again, given this was conducted between 2009 and 2014, it’s not hard to imagine these patients with prior suicide attempts and self-injury couldn’t find help. It’s hard to get access to care in 2025 with suicidality, but at least DBT, MBT, and other therapies are now more mainstream.

The DBT Therapy was evaluated by video, and judged to be highly adherent to the model:

All DBT therapists were Ph.D. clinical psychologists trained by the Behavioral Technology Transfer Group. They attended weekly DBT consultation team meetings. All sessions were video recorded, and 10% were randomly selected and coded for adherence …Therapists received an average rating of 4.1 on a scale of 1–5, with adherence indicated by a score ≥4.0.

All psychologist (doctoral-level) therapy limits the generalizability a bit—this majority of therapists are masters level clinicians—but for the purposes of this study, it demonstrates the DBT therapy was absolutely what they thought it was.

The SSRI/M group was more intensive treatment than most patients get, it’s also worth noting:

For those randomized to SSRI/M, fluoxetine was started at 20mg/day, and the maximum dosage was set at 40mg/day, because higher dosages are not more effective for treating depression ….Participants attended 30-minute sessions with the psychiatrist at a minimum frequency of every 2 weeks; the sessions were weekly if the participant’s condition worsened. They received psychoeducation and general support…A social worker was available on request for clinical management and support, as recommended by Fawcett et al. (27).

30 minutes with an MD at least every two weeks? This is a lot of treatment in America! We have good data, from John Gunderson, that “good enough” psychiatric managmemnt of BPD is non-inferior to DBT in prior studies, when it comes to suicidal behavior.3

The authors don’t provide details on what the psychoeducational consisted of. Even if it were perfectly aligned with GPM, it would make the outcome of this study all the more surprising.

Crucially, the DBT arm was not given SSRI medication, just the therapy after “washout of their prior medication.”

The endpoints?

The primary preregistered analysis was the comparison of the number of suicide-related events (SREs) over the 6-month treatment phase. Secondary self-harm outcome measures were the occur- rence of, time to, and number of 1) suicide attempts and 2) NSSI behaviors during the study.

They used a methodology I happen to adore for this study— “time-to-event” survival analysis (which I previously explained in more detail here). They find that These two treatments are very different, and SSRIs, even with Clincal Management is definitively worse:

The above shows the difference between all suicide related events, and the following analysis only looks at suicide attempts, which are also demonstrably worse in the SSRI/M group:

Two points to make, from your author, interpreting this data:

  1. SSRI/M, if it is anywhere close to GPM, is an active and effective treatment for BPD (Referencing the prior trial on the Gunderson Manualized Good Psychiatric Management (amazon affiliate link) by McMann et. al.):

Thus, the difference here is that the DBT group isn’t on an SSRI, and the SSRI/M group is likely getting a non-inferior therapy plus something deleterious in the Prozac.

That is to say, either DBT is preventing suicide better than SSRI/M, OR SSRIs, when added to “/M” clinical care, may be HARMFUL to BPD patients and increase rates of suicide attempt and self-harm because it’s been established previously that GPM, which looks a lot like “/M,” is non-inferior to DBT.

This study doesn’t include a third arm that would allow us to tell if DBT is good or SSRIs are bad. Both could be true. It’s already a frighteningly hard study to run, as evidenced by the many years it took to publish this paper, so I don’t blame them.

  1. The second takeaway is more pedantic, but this data makes it hard to argue that structured management, which includes the GPM model's recommendation to “offer the SSRI,” should continue to include it. This trial allowed meds for sleep, including Ambien and benzos, which I would not prescribe for BPD patients in this day and age, in both groups. So it’s not drugs or no drugs— “/M” is specifically worse than DBT AND NO SSRIs in that it leads to more suicide attempts. Benzos alone are already associated with more deaths by suicide4; it’s worth remembering.

But maybe, just maybe, the black box warning of SSRIs for adolescents should extend to BPD patients also? And maybe, just maybe, the risk of suicidal ideation from SSRIs in adolescents might be best understood as a risk that is based on underlying variability and…wait for it…maybe those kids, the more suicidal ones, had BPD in those theoretically depression studies?

In summary, this data, to your author Owen Muir, provides yet more rationale to encourage DBT and other non-pharmacological treatments for BPD. This, as always, means we need more robust reimbursement for a treatment that is expensive to train in and to provide… but plausibly life-saving. It’s also the case that psychiatrists should consider never prescribing prozac and plausibly other SSRIs to patients with BPD. We have data that the drugs don’t work over and over again, and here, they are worse than therapy alone.

BPD patients deserve better than a hurried prescription and a caring follow-up. They deserve definitive care— and that means therapy, and perhaps treatments like TMS for their depression, not plausibly-suicide-risk-increasing drugs.

Health plans? Update your prior authorization standards and treatment algorithms accordingly!

Or Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons, but nothing is close to significant, so this point doesn’t matter in this context.

2

Black, D. W., Zanarini, M. C., Romine, A., Shaw, M., Allen, J., & Schulz, S. C. (2014). Comparison of low and moderate dosages of extended-release quetiapine in borderline personality disorder: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. American Journal of Psychiatry, 171(11), 1174-1182.

3

McMain, S. F., Links, P. S., Gnam, W. H., Guimond, T., Cardish, R. J., Korman, L., & Streiner, D. L. (2009). A randomized trial of dialectical behavior therapy versus general psychiatric management for borderline personality disorder. american Journal of Psychiatry, 166(12), 1365-1374.

4

Cato, V., Holländare, F., Nordenskjöld, A. et al. Association between benzodiazepines and suicide risk: a matched case-control study. BMC Psychiatry 19, 317 (2019). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-019-2312-3

Dodds TJ. Prescribed Benzodiazepines and Suicide Risk: A Review of the Literature. Prim Care Companion CNS Disord. 2017 Mar 2;19(2). doi: 10.4088/PCC.16r02037. PMID: 28257172.
